south dakota.adverse_possession_note: Possession must be actual, open and notorious (visible), exclusive, continuous, and hostile (without the owner's permission) for 20 years. The period drops to 10 years if the claimant has color of title (a deed or other document that looks like ownership but is legally flawed) AND has paid the property taxes for those 10 years. The claim is not automatic — the claimant must go to court to quiet title. Governed by S.D. Codified Laws §§ 15-3-1, 15-3-15 and 15-3-16.
south dakota.agency_name: South Dakota Unified Judicial System — Legal Self-Help
south dakota.easement_by_necessity_note: Yes — South Dakota recognizes easements by necessity. If a parcel is landlocked with no legal access to a public road, a court may grant an easement across a neighbor's land so the property can be reached, even if the neighbor objects.
south dakota.prescriptive_easement_note: A prescriptive easement is the right to keep using someone else's land for a specific purpose (such as driving on a road or path) after 20 years of open, visible, continuous, unmolested use without the owner's permission. Unlike adverse possession, it gives only a right to use the land, not ownership of it. You cannot get a prescriptive easement against government-owned land.
south dakota.state_note: South Dakota's 20-year period is among the longest in the country, and it is one of the few states where paying taxes plus holding a deed actually shortens the clock. Western South Dakota is served by a separate program, Dakota Plains Legal Services, and the statewide intake portal is SD Law Help.
south dakota.statute_name: South Dakota Codified Laws, Chapter 15-3 (Adverse Possession and Limitation of Actions to Recover Real Estate)

tennessee.adverse_possession_note: Possession must be actual, open and notorious, exclusive, continuous, hostile (without permission), and under a claim of right for 20 years. The period drops to 7 years if the claimant holds color of title — a recorded deed or document that appears to give ownership but is legally defective — recorded for the full 7 years. A claimant who never pays property taxes is vulnerable: under Tenn. Code § 28-2-110, a person who fails to have the land assessed and pay taxes on it for more than 20 years is barred from recovering it.
tennessee.agency_name: Tennessee Bar Association — For the Public
tennessee.easement_by_necessity_note: Yes — Tennessee recognizes easements by necessity (and easements by prior use). A landlocked parcel can get court-ordered access over a neighbor's land, but the claimant must prove the access is genuinely necessary, not merely convenient, and the necessity must have existed when the land was divided (Cowan v. Hardeman County).
tennessee.legal_aid_name: Legal Aid Society of Middle Tennessee and the Cumberlands
tennessee.prescriptive_easement_note: A prescriptive easement is earned by 20 continuous years of open, adverse use of another person's land under a claim of right — for example, driving across a neighbor's land to reach your own. It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose, not ownership. Use with the owner's permission never counts, and simply using a road without objection is not enough without proof of a hostile claim of right.
tennessee.state_note: Tennessee has four regional legal aid programs; the Legal Aid Society of Middle Tennessee and the Cumberlands is the state's largest nonprofit law firm, serving 48 counties. East Tennessee is served by Legal Aid of East Tennessee and West Tennessee by West Tennessee Legal Services and Memphis Area Legal Services.
tennessee.statute_name: Tennessee Code Annotated, Title 28, Chapter 2 (Limitation of Actions — Real Property)

texas.adverse_possession_note: Texas has a ladder of periods, not one number. The standard period with no deed at all is 10 years of peaceable possession while cultivating, using, or enjoying the land (capped at 160 acres without a title document). It is 3 years with title or color of title, 5 years with a duly registered deed plus paying the property taxes, and 25 years in special cases (including claims against an owner under a legal disability). Possession must be actual and visible, hostile to the owner's claim, and continuous. Since 2021, the 5-year route does not apply to quitclaim deeds, forged deeds, or deeds signed under a forged power of attorney.
texas.easement_by_necessity_note: Yes — Texas recognizes easements by necessity, but being landlocked alone is not enough. The claimant must prove three things: the two parcels were once owned by the same person, the access is a true necessity (not a mere convenience), and the necessity existed when the parcels were split (Hamrick v. Ward, 2014). A landlocked owner can also ask the county commissioners court for a public access road under Texas Transportation Code § 251.053.
texas.prescriptive_easement_note: A prescriptive easement is gained by at least 10 years of use that is open and notorious, continuous, exclusive, and adverse (without permission) — the same 10-year period as the general adverse possession statute. It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose (such as a driveway), not ownership. Texas courts disfavor these claims and scrutinize every element strictly.
texas.state_note: Texas has three main regional legal aid programs: Lone Star Legal Aid (Houston and East Texas, 72 counties), Legal Aid of NorthWest Texas (114 counties in North and West Texas), and Texas RioGrande Legal Aid (South Texas). The State Bar's Lawyer Referral & Information Service offers a 30-minute consultation for $20.
texas.statute_name: Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code, Chapter 16, Subchapter B (Limitations of Real Property Actions)

utah.adverse_possession_note: Utah requires 7 years of continuous, open, hostile possession — but with a strict condition most states do not impose: the claimant must have paid ALL property taxes levied and assessed on the land for the entire 7-year period (Utah Code § 78B-2-209). Color of title (a document that appears to convey ownership) is also part of the statutory scheme. The owner is presumed to be in possession until the claimant proves 7 years of adverse holding (§ 78B-2-208).
utah.agency_name: Utah State Bar — Tips on Finding a Utah Attorney
utah.easement_by_necessity_note: Yes — Utah recognizes easements by necessity for landlocked parcels. The claimant must show the two parcels were once under common ownership, the access is truly necessary (not merely convenient), and the necessity existed when the parcels were split. The easement ends if the necessity ends, for example if another public road reaches the property.
utah.prescriptive_easement_note: A prescriptive easement in Utah takes 20 years — much longer than the 7-year adverse possession period. The claimant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the use was open, notorious, adverse (without permission), and continuous for at least 20 years (Utah Code § 78B-2-206; Van Denburgh v. Sweeney Land Co.). It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose, not ownership. Use shared with the general public is presumed permissive, not adverse. A separate statute covers prescriptive easements for water conveyances (§ 57-13a-102, also 20 years).
utah.state_note: Utah is unusual: its adverse possession period (7 years) is one of the shortest in the country, but its prescriptive easement period (20 years) is nearly three times longer. Since May 7, 2025, a Utah owner can also ask police to remove a trespasser on a verified complaint without a court case (S.B. 55, Utah Code § 78B-6-817).
utah.statute_name: Utah Code, Title 78B, Chapter 2, Part 2 (Adverse Possession)

vermont.adverse_possession_note: Possession must be open, notorious, hostile (without permission), exclusive, and continuous for 15 years (12 V.S.A. § 501). Vermont does NOT require color of title or payment of property taxes. The claimant must then file a quiet title action in Superior Court and prove every element; ownership does not transfer automatically. One exception: a buyer at a tax sale who records the deed, moves in, and pays taxes gives the former owner only 1 year to sue (32 V.S.A. § 5263).
vermont.easement_by_necessity_note: Yes — Vermont recognizes easements by necessity (implied easements) for landlocked parcels. But there is a catch: in Gray v. Treder (2018), the Vermont Supreme Court held that an unrecorded easement by necessity can be wiped out by the state's Marketable Record Title Act, so an access easement should be recorded to survive.
vermont.prescriptive_easement_note: A prescriptive easement is established by open, notorious, continuous, and adverse use of another's land for 15 years, which creates a presumption of a claim of right (Russell v. Pare; Community Feed Store v. Northeast Culvert Corp.). It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose — for example, a road or a path to a lake — not ownership. Permission from the owner defeats the claim, and successive owners can combine (tack) their periods of use if there is privity between them.
vermont.state_note: Vermont Legal Aid works together with Legal Services Vermont (formerly Law Line); both share the VTLawHelp.org intake system. The Vermont Bar Association's Lawyer Referral Service offers a 30-minute consultation for no more than $25.
vermont.statute_name: Vermont Statutes Annotated, Title 12, Chapter 23 (Limitation of Time for Commencement of Actions)

virginia.adverse_possession_note: Possession must be actual, hostile, exclusive, visible (open and notorious), and continuous, under a claim of right, for 15 years (Va. Code § 8.01-236). The claimant must prove every element by clear and convincing evidence — a high bar — and Virginia courts presume that someone occupying another's land does so with permission. You cannot adversely possess land owned by the federal or state government. Successive possessors can combine (tack) their time only if there is privity, such as a deed connecting them.
virginia.easement_by_necessity_note: Yes — Virginia recognizes easements by necessity for landlocked parcels. The claimant must show the two parcels were once under common ownership, the land became landlocked when the land was divided, and there is currently no other way in or out. Mere convenience is not enough, and if another route later becomes available the neighbor can ask a court to end the easement.
virginia.prescriptive_easement_note: Virginia is unusual: a prescriptive easement takes 20 years, longer than the 15-year adverse possession period. The claimant must show use that was adverse, under a claim of right, exclusive, continuous and uninterrupted, with the landowner's knowledge, for at least 20 years (Craig v. Kennedy, 202 Va. 654; Powell v. Magee). It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose, not ownership. A separate statute defines prescriptive easements for utility and communications providers as 20 years or more (Va. Code § 55.1-306.1).
virginia.state_note: Virginia has several regional legal aid programs (Central, Southwest, Eastern Virginia, Northern Virginia, Blue Ridge); Virginia Legal Aid Society serves 20 counties and 6 cities in Central, Southside, and Western Tidewater Virginia. Virginia also has a court process to relocate a longstanding easement (10 years or older) under Va. Code § 55.1-304.
virginia.statute_name: Code of Virginia, Title 8.01, Chapter 4 (Limitation of entry on or action for land)

washington.adverse_possession_note: Possession must be hostile (without permission), actual, exclusive, open and notorious, and continuous for 10 years (RCW 4.16.020). The period drops to 7 years if the claimant holds the land under color of title (a deed that appears valid) or has paid the property taxes (RCW 7.28.070). No adverse possession claim can be made against state or other government-owned land, and forestland claims also require substantial improvements that stayed on the land for at least 10 years (RCW 7.28.085).
washington.agency_name: Washington State Bar Association — Find Legal Help
washington.easement_by_necessity_note: Yes — Washington recognizes easements by necessity (ways of necessity) for landlocked land, but the bar is strict necessity, not reasonable necessity — poor access alone does not qualify. Washington also has a private condemnation statute (RCW 8.24.010) letting a landlocked owner condemn a private way of necessity and pay the neighbor for it.
washington.prescriptive_easement_note: A prescriptive easement requires 10 years of use that is open and notorious, continuous and uninterrupted, over a uniform route, adverse to the owner, and with the owner's knowledge at a time when the owner could have enforced their rights (Gamboa v. Clark, 183 Wn.2d 38). It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose, not ownership. Washington presumes that a neighbor's use of a road is permissive (neighborly accommodation), so the claimant must overcome that presumption.
washington.state_note: Washington's free legal help runs through the CLEAR intake line (outside King County) and 211 (inside King County), both coordinated by the Northwest Justice Project, which also runs WashingtonLawHelp.org. The state bar itself does not refer people to private attorneys; it points to county bar referral services instead.
washington.statute_name: Revised Code of Washington, Title 4, Chapter 4.16 and Title 7, Chapter 7.28 (Adverse Possession)

west virginia.adverse_possession_note: Possession must be hostile (adverse), actual, open and notorious, exclusive, continuous, and under claim of title or color of title for 10 years (W. Va. Code § 55-2-1; Elder v. Smith). If the true owner was a minor or mentally incapacitated when the occupation began, they get 5 extra years after the disability ends to sue (§ 55-2-3). A 2025 bill to abolish adverse possession (HB 2924) was introduced but did not become law, so the 10-year rule still stands.
west virginia.agency_name: West Virginia Lawyer Referral Service (West Virginia State Bar)
west virginia.easement_by_necessity_note: Yes — West Virginia recognizes easements by necessity, called a 'way of necessity.' Under Cobb v. Daugherty, the claimant must prove four things: both properties were once under common ownership, a conveyance split them apart, the easement was strictly necessary for the landlocked parcel at the time of the split, and the necessity continues today. The easement ends when the necessity ends, such as when a new road reaches the property.
west virginia.prescriptive_easement_note: A prescriptive easement requires open, continuous and uninterrupted use of a road or path over another's land, under a bona fide claim of right and without the owner's objection, for 10 years (Holland v. Flanagan; O'Dell v. Stegall). The claimant must prove each element by clear and convincing evidence, including the reasonably precise location, width, and purpose of the use. It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose, not ownership, and use with the owner's permission never counts.
west virginia.state_note: West Virginia's 2025 Stop Squatters Act (W. Va. Code §§ 55-3C-1 to 55-3C-6, in effect July 10, 2025) lets a property owner ask police to remove a squatter on a verified complaint without an eviction case; squatting is treated as criminal trespass, not a tenancy. Legal Aid of West Virginia is the state's primary civil legal aid provider, with 12 offices statewide.
west virginia.statute_name: West Virginia Code, Chapter 55, Article 2 (Limitation of Actions and Suits)

wisconsin.adverse_possession_note: The standard period with no deed is 20 years of uninterrupted adverse possession, and the land must be actually occupied and either protected by a substantial enclosure (such as a fence) or usually cultivated or improved (Wis. Stat. § 893.25). It drops to 10 years with a recorded written instrument (color of title, § 893.26) and to 7 years with color of title plus payment of taxes (§ 893.27). There is no good-faith requirement for the 20-year route. No adverse possession against state or local government land except after 20+ years on a mutually agreed fence line (§ 893.29).
wisconsin.agency_name: State Bar of Wisconsin — Lawyer Referral Service
wisconsin.easement_by_necessity_note: Yes — Wisconsin recognizes a common-law way of necessity for landlocked parcels, but it is granted through the circuit court's discretion, not automatically as a matter of law (McCormick v. Schubring, 2003 WI 149). A landlocked owner can also apply to the town board to have a public highway laid out to the property under Wis. Stat. § 82.27, with the owner paying the cost.
wisconsin.prescriptive_easement_note: A prescriptive easement requires continuous adverse use of another person's land for at least 20 years (Wis. Stat. § 893.28(1)). The use must be hostile and inconsistent with the owner's rights, visible, open and notorious, under an open claim of right, and continuous and uninterrupted for the full 20 years (Bauer v. Wisconsin Energy Corp.). It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose, not ownership. A shorter 10-year period applies only to certain utilities and cooperatives (§ 893.28(2)), and use of a way over unenclosed (wild, unimproved) land is presumed permissive, not adverse (§ 893.28(3)). Once the right accrues, the holder must record it within 30 years or lose it (§ 893.33(2)).
wisconsin.state_note: Legal Action of Wisconsin merged with Judicare Legal Aid on January 1, 2026, so it is now the single statewide civil legal aid intake for the whole state. The State Bar's Lawyer Referral Service charges no more than $20 for a first 30-minute consultation.
wisconsin.statute_name: Wisconsin Statutes, Chapter 893, Subchapter III (Adverse Possession and Prescription)

wyoming.adverse_possession_note: Possession must be actual, open, notorious, continuous, exclusive, and hostile (adverse to the owner's interest) for 10 years (Wyo. Stat. § 1-3-103). Wyoming has no shortcut: the statute does not shorten the period for paying taxes or holding a deed, so a claimant with no paperwork is on the same 10-year clock as anyone else. A 2025 bill that would have stopped the clock while the owner paid all property taxes (HB 123) passed the House but died in a Senate committee, so the flat 10 years stands.
wyoming.easement_by_necessity_note: Yes — Wyoming recognizes implied easements, including easements by prior use where a road or path was openly used before the land was split (Hansuld v. Lariat Diesel Corp.). Wyoming also has a statutory private road remedy: a landlocked owner can petition the court for a private road of necessity under Wyo. Stat. § 24-9-101, paying the neighbor damages — confirmed in Wagonhound Land & Livestock Co. v. Little Medicine Creek Ranch (2026).
wyoming.prescriptive_easement_note: A prescriptive easement in Wyoming takes 10 years of use that is continuous and uninterrupted, open and notorious, and adverse (without permission) — the same period as adverse possession. It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose, not ownership. The 10-year period is codified for water conveyances in Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-158 (2023), which also lets the holder file a notice of the easement with the county clerk.
wyoming.state_note: Since July 1, 2025, Wyoming law (SF 6, Enrolled Act 20) lets a property owner apply to law enforcement to remove an unauthorized occupant from a residence without first going to court. Legal Aid of Wyoming runs a free Legal Aid Hotline staffed by licensed attorneys, and Equal Justice Wyoming (equaljustice.wy.gov) is the state's legal-help website.
wyoming.statute_name: Wyoming Statutes, Title 1, Chapter 3 (Limitation of Actions — Recovery of Real Property)
